citations.verbatim_quote: Indeed, in my view, both 'Hopping John' and 'jamboree' were likely coined in roughly the same place and period, namely in southern Alabama near the beginning of the nineteenth century, in a context of increasing Anglo-French Creole contact ... 'Jamboree' is then the word 'jambalaya' borrowed and phonologically adapted into the English of Anglophone African-American communities of the southeast, clearly akin to some variants of 'jambalaya' attested from areas peripheral to the French-speaking Gulf Coast or from non-French-speakers, most notably 'jumberlie' and 'jambolin'
citations.linguistic_note: Anthony F. Buccini's Provençal *jambalalha / jambaraia / jambalaia -> Gulf Coast French Creole jambalaya -> southeastern African-American / American English jamboree hypothesis
citations.analysis_notes: Full scholarly credit and critical audit of linguist and food historian Anthony F. Buccini's Provençal-to-Gulf-Creole donor hypothesis (post-1930 scholarship: scan_inspected=False, scan_evidence_filename=None per pre-1931 gate). Strengths verified by our primary scans: (1) exact consonant-skeleton identity between Provençal jambaraia/jambalaia (SNPL) and English jamboree (SNPL, edit distance 0), reinforced by Mobile oral Creole Jumberlie (1881, SNPL); (2) striking semantic match in Chailan's 1837/1840 Marseille verse ('fasien chavararin ... Ero un jambaraya de fachos de cenobre', drunken noisy crowd); and (3) pre-1858 Gulf presence of jambalaya (May 1849) alongside charivari -> shevaree (-aree/-oree stress shift). Critical geographic-chronological tension identified: Buccini (2018, n. 18) posits that 'jamboree must have spread to the north of the US in the wake of the Civil War' (citing 1873 McKee and 1880 Angelo), overlooking that jamboree is already attested before the Civil War in June 1858 Kings County (Brooklyn)/New York courtroom and volunteer-fireman slang ('noisy drinking bout') while remaining unattested as jamboree in antebellum Louisiana/Alabama print. Any Gulf Creole input into jamboree therefore required antebellum coastal packet, riverboat, or minstrel transmission to New York before 1858 and/or convergent remodeling on the productive American -oree/-aree template. Cross-shard duplicate of Buccini 2017 Dublin Gastronomy Symposium / 2018 Oxford Symposium Provençal 'jambaraia' paper (S09 CERT-2500-906 merged here).

Consequently, Zola Sohna's (2019) Mandinka jomboroo hypothesis, which relies heavily on that unverified 1854 'festival/fete' abstract, lacks primary antebellum semantic corroboration.
